title: The Rules for Rulers (now titled: Try to Rule Fairly and You'll Be Overthrown)
subject: Political science
beats: Casts you as an aspiring ruler: do you want to rule and fix your country?
Why do rulers act selfishly and stupidly? Are they dumb, or is it something else?
No one rules alone: power is getting others to act; names keys to power
In a dictatorship the keys are few, maybe a dozen generals and officials
All countries sit on a spectrum from few keys to many
Rule 1: get key supporters. Rule 2: control the treasure
You, benevolent dictator, want to help citizens, but that hands rivals a weapon
Keys face the same problem one level down, so loyalty must be bought
The self-sustaining core: court raises treasure, treasure keeps the court
Many keys shorten reigns; Rule 3: minimize key supporters
Why does a new dictator purge his allies? The rules make it obvious
Excited or exhausted? Turn to democracy
Democracy: same rules, power fractured among many
Voters are bought as blocks: elderly, homeowners, farmers
Farm subsidies follow how key the farm vote is
Non-voting blocks get nothing; Rule 3 applies again: gerrymanders, voting rules
Big individual keys get loopholes and contracts, not gold
Corruption is a tool; contradictory-looking actions balance keys
Why not just bribe the army? Turn to taxes and revolts
Graph: more keys, lower tax rates
You may scoff, but low earners pull the average down; dictators take wealth directly
Democracies tax less because productive citizens make more treasure
Democracies are better not because leaders are better but because incentives align
Resource-rich dictatorships are the worst: mines run without citizens
Stable democracies, stable resource dictatorships, a valley of revolution between
Romantic popular revolts are mostly fantasy: the court replaces the king
Why benevolent dictators fail to cross the valley
Why coups fail in stable democracies: the gamble and the math
When democracies fall: poverty or a resource that dwarfs citizen productivity
The rules explain war, aid, dynasties, corruption, CEOs, HOAs
Zeroth rule: without power you affect nothing; maybe you'll be different

meta.notation_note: No notation. Its 'interface' is a numbered rule set (rules 1-3, plus a zeroth rule at the end) and one chart at 10:29.
meta.misconception: yes: 0:15 (rulers are just stupid), 2:25 (benevolence is safe), 14:04 (people overthrow kings). Broken from 0:47 onward.
meta.examples: many: dictatorship, coups, democracy blocks, farm subsidies, resource states, middling dictators, stable democracies, CEOs and HOAs
meta.examples_grow: same 3 rules repeated across settings of growing complexity: king, dictatorship, democracy, any organization
meta.ending: generalize to every organization + callback to the second-person ruler hook with a zeroth rule
